editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Today is Thursday, March 13, 2003, and this is the beginning of an interview with Howard Finley Bolton at the Erlanger Halfway Plus Office, 975 East Third Street, Chattanooga, Tennessee. Mr. Bolton was born on [birth date redacted], and is now 78 years old. My name is Michael Willie and I will conduct this interview. Mr. Bolton, could you state for the recording your name and its spelling, please.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Howard Finley Bolton. That's H-o-w-a-r-d, Finley, F-i-n-l-e-y, Bolton, B-o-l-t-o-n.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And during which years did you serve?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: I served from 1941, May 1941 until September 1962.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And in which branch of the service?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: I was in the army.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And what was your highest rank attained?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Chief warrant officer, W-2.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Where were you born, Mr. Bolton?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Born in Chaska, Tennessee. That's a little coal mining town above Knoxville.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And tell me about your family. Do you have any brothers and sisters?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yes, I did. There were nine in my family, and I'm next -- there's two younger than me. During the war I had a younger brother in the navy and I had two older brothers. One was in tanks in Fort Bragg, the other was in amphibious boat landing craft up at Fort Devens, Massachusetts. He later went to the Pacific and did a lot of assault landings over there. And the others were sisters and obviously they were not in the war.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And what about your parents, your dad? What's your dad do?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: My dad was a railroad conductor on the L and N, and he had about 30 years service. He died shortly before I went in the army. My mother, he met my mother up in that coal country between Knoxville and Corbin near that little town of Chaska where I was born. And most of my brothers and sisters were born in those coal mining towns up there where the railroad was very active at that time and my father worked.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Now, you say you were born there. Then did you move around at all?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yes, we did. My family moved to Knoxville when I was quite small, and we went to school in Knoxville. And I did not complete school there. I left school in ninth grade.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: How old were you at that time?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: I was 15, I think. And I went out west for a while and worked with one of my brothers out there in the timber. And that didn't work out too well; too cold, too hard work. I came back to Knoxville and I worked at some menial jobs; worked in the drug stores and that sort of thing, rode a motorcycle delivering prescriptions for a drugstore in Knoxville. And then right after my dad died I went in the army.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Because your dad died?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yes. I wanted his permission to go and he never would give me his permission to go in. And I really wanted to go because all my friends and people I knew in the neighborhood and so forth were going in the service at that time. We were flag waving back then and everybody expected war.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: And the mobile guard had already been nationalized. And so after he died I was lost. I didn't know where to go and what to do and so I went in the service.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And what about your mom? What was she doing at that time?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Well, she was a housekeeper, a very good one. But with all the children we had, she was a mother, wife, housekeeper all our life.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: But after your dad died how did she --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: She stayed there. And all of us kept in touch with her during the war, sent her a little money each month and so forth. And then during the war she took in some roomers. Roomers, that's --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Hard to understand.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yeah. She took in some boarders that were working in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, they were building that at that time, a big secret project, and a place to live was hard to find in Knoxville. So she did that, picked up a little money.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. So you joined the army. At that point are your brothers already in --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- the service? They hadn't gone in yet?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So you join. And where do you go for induction?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: I joined in Knoxville and was sent immediately to Fort Oglethorpe, Georgia. At that time the Calvary unit was still out there, the Calvary regiment, the 12th, I believe it was. And it was real interesting to me. I had never been around anything like that. And we did a little bit of basic training down there. Actually, they took a lot of us that were going into the service at that time and gave us a little basic training, mostly to keep us busy and introduce us to the army and so forth. And they worked us to death, we really had to work out there. Those Calvary men were glad to see the ground-pounders-to-be put to work mowing their grass and so forth. It was interesting. They jumped all over us for calling their horses horses. They let us know right away that those were not horses, they were United States Government mounts. And very interesting. We got introduced to the chit system where you could get a little book, get so many packs of cigarettes a month or so many beers or a hair cut and that sort of thing. They called it the chit system, and common language for it in the army was jawboning. So if you were going to the orderly room to get books you were going down to jawbone. So I would like to have stayed out there, it was a beautiful post and it was an ideal place. But we only stayed there long enough to do a lot of work and then we shipped off to Camp Croft, North Carolina -- South Carolina, I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Did you say Camp Cross?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yeah, C-r-o-f-t.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Camp Croft, okay.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yes. And that was an infantry training center.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Give me your first impressions when you show up here, when you show up at Camp Croft for basic training. You've had just a taste of military life at Fort Oglethorpe and now you get into Camp Croft. How is that the same and how is that different?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Well, we came in on a train, a special car. We got on a special train in Chattanooga and went to Atlanta, and from Atlanta another special car, changed trains, and went to South Carolina. When we got there, there were a few officers standing on the platform and a few non-commissioned officers but nobody else. There was no bands playing or anything like that. And the odd thing about it was there were no vehicles. There was a couple, maybe two or three ambulance out there, civilian-type ambulance, and but they were painted OD, army drab. And that was odd, there was nothing there. We were just out in the woods. So we could see in the distance where the railroad did extend to the barracks that it was at least a half mile, probably three-quarters, to those barracks. So we had to carry our new issue of clothing that we got at Fort Oglethorpe, we had to carry all those things in the hot sun and go to those barracks and we were assigned the space. The thing I remember most about Camp Croft was that while we were waiting for these units to fill up where they would have a training battalion and enough people to get started with a training program, we had work details every day. The work details for a good while were building the parade ground. We built a parade ground out of a reasonably flat place. There had been some cornfields out there but a lot of it was pine thickets. And we built that by hand. There was no bulldozers, no front-end loaders, no dump trucks, no chain saws, nothing like that. So with just manpower and brand-new blue fatigue uniforms with a big floppy hat that you've seen, we worked in the hot Carolina sun out there and pull the trees, we'd dig around the trees. And we'd put 40 men on a long rope and pull a stump out of the ground, and then another crew of men would come in and shovel and fill the hole up. And we had some that raked it and graded it. Well, in three to four months we had the most beautiful parade ground in the United States Army.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Something to be proud of?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Well, we got to parade on it. Our final parade before we shipped out of there was on that parade ground. I wasn't proud of it so much but glad to leave it.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: {Laughter} Any time during there where you thought you might have made a decision joining the service?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: No. No, I liked the service. I had a fine first sergeant there and a fine company commander. The first sergeant was one of the finest soldiers I ever met, and this was in basic training. I never knew him personally, he wasn't that kind of soldier. You couldn't get next to him. His mother couldn't kiss him, I don't believe. But anyhow, he impressed me quite a bit. And our company commander would really jump on us if we were goofing around. And he told us several times you better pay attention to what you're doing because you're going to be using those bayonets and those rifles pretty soon. And at 17 years it didn't impress you much. But he was absolutely right. And we worked hard and we got some good training down there. And after we left there, I went to Fort Dix, New Jersey.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Around what time of the year is this?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: This is getting around, let's see, May, June, July, last of August.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Last of August?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So the draft has already been instated at this point? I mean, did you notice an influx of --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: No, I don't know the draft -- yes, the draft was going at that time. And a lot of Nashville Guard had been mobilized, and I had the bad fortune of being assigned to a National Guard regiment in Fort Dix. It was the 44th Infantry Division and I was 113th Infantry. It also had a sister regiment there, the 114th Infantry, the 113th and the 114th. And these were the old division system where you had a lot more men in a division and a regiment and a squad and so forth than you do now. There were a lot of men in the infantry. And right after we got there we had very little time to do anything except get familiar with the place and more training. We went on the maneuver, which I still refer to as the Carolina Maneuver, was the largest maneuver that was ever held in the eastern part of the United States. And they had the red army and the blue army, and there were troops there from South Carolina and Louisiana and Georgia and there were troops from Pennsylvania, all up in the New England states. There was troops from all over the army were there. It was a huge maneuver. And it was pitiful. And I know that you've seen stories about it that we didn't have the equipment we needed. They'd put the word "tank" on the side of a truck to indicate that that was a tank attack and that sort of thing. In the infantry we didn't have to do that. We had all the infantry weapons that we were ever going to get.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yeah, we had plenty of that. We had -- I was first assigned to a heavy weapons company, the F Company, and we had 81-millimeter mortars and we had 50-caliber machine guns, 30-caliber machine guns in the heavy weapons company.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. But as far as the rest of the troops that are there, are there plenty of -- well, what kind of rifles are they using? Are these the M1 --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: The M1 was not out at that time. We had basic training on the 03, the Springfield. It was a fine rifle in World War I, but we did not have that kind of equipment. In fact, in that maneuver all the troops still had the old-type helmet like the British have. I won't tell you what we called those, but we called it a pot. You can use your imagination there. But we had old-style equipment. We had wrap leggings. Instead of putting your leggings on and either zipping them or hook fasteners on them you had to wrap continuously around your ankles and up the calf of your leg until you got the leggings on. And when you're a recruit, if you can keep them on going 30 paces then you're becoming a soldier. {Laughter}

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: {Laughter} And how did the maneuvers go? How did everyone react together? I mean, were there --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: We were all lost and confused. We would get in a truck and ride 30, 40, 50 miles to some town and we'd never know whether we saw the enemy or the enemy saw us. We were never critiqued on what happened. And very few people cared. They were all anxious to get back home. And the outfit I was in, 113th, was a New Jersey National Guard outfit that they were from around Trenton, Patterson and Newark and all through Jersey. And they were all homeboys, apparently. That's all they could think about. They were not very good soldiers, some of them. They became that. And on the way back from the Carolina Maneuvers in South Boston, Virginia, we were in bivouac there, we pulled into some farmer's pasture and set up our tents and a kitchen. And late on a -- I can't remember whether it was a Sunday night or it was late on the Monday, must have been that Sunday night, we got the word that Pearl Harbor had been hit. And so the question was who was Pearl Harbor? We didn't know she was around. And everybody wanted to know where is Pearl Harbor. We didn't know anything about Pearl Harbor. But then after we got a few more details the writing was on the walls. All those people that were so anxious to get home started worrying about not getting home. And of course, many of them did who lived close to Fort Dix because that's where we went. But we were at Fort Dix and it was getting cold weather. And the war was on, it was a big emergency, we didn't know what we were going to do. And the regiment was split up at that time. Incidentally, our commanding officer of that regiment was Norman Schwarzkopf, the father of the famous Norman Schwarzkopf in Desert Storm. And he was a fine infantry officer. Some people might remember him being famous for his participation in the Lindbergh case. So the regiment broke up then, and some of us went to Long Island and some of us went to down around Asbury Park and so forth. But we went to Mitchell Field, Long Island first with the half-ton weapons carriers with the 30-caliber machine gun pointing up in the air and freezing to death out there on that flat runway and the wind and the breeze coming right off the ocean. And we didn't know what we were shooting at, who to look for. You would have thought they were expecting Hitler himself to come down the road or come flying in in an airplane. But that didn't last very long. But it was a stupid thing, looking back on it, to put soldiers out with machine guns pointing up in the air when war had hardly been declared.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: But the rest of the regiment was spread out up and down the coast, and we moved from there to Woodbine, New Jersey. And from there we occupied an old CCC camp. I guess you know what that is?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: No. Let's talk about what an old CCC camp is.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Civilian Conservation Corps. It was one of the letter programs under Roosevelt, and it was to get the use of America back to work. And so they organized them into platoons and squads just like the army. And they did work, they built parks, federal parks, and active in helping the Forestry Service, that sort of thing. It's a good thing they had them because it was easy to induct all these men into the army when they needed them. But the regiment was walking beach patrol {Coughs} -- pardon me, and the beach patrol was watching for anything suspicious to come in from the ocean. There was restrictions on lights at night. All the lights facing the ocean had to be extinguished to dark so it wouldn't silhouette the ships out in the ocean. Ships were sailing from New York and going south along the Jersey coast, and the lights from the shore would silhouette those ships. And the German U-Boats were very active off the coast, so our job was to keep those lights out. And it was an interesting job. The people seemed to appreciate it. They really treated us nice out there.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: How did you do that? Are you just walking the beach?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: We had one BAR, Browning Automatic Rifle, and one M1 -- did we have M1's? I can't remember if we had the M1 or the 03 then. But anyhow, we walked the beach in two shifts from dusk to dark, and from -- I can't remember the hours that we walked. But anyhow, we walked up and down the beach and watched for the lights and to keep people off the beach. A lot of people in cars would just drive their car up toward the beach and leave their headlights on out in the water, and we'd ask them to turn their lights out. And everybody obeyed, we didn't have any problems. We didn't need any sort of police powers or anything. But we carried a raincoat called a light pack, a rain coat and a canteen, an ammunition belt, rifle, helmet, and a mosquito net, which you really needed. And we walked the patrol. And all the ladies up in the beach houses there would bring goodies down to the soldiers. They'd bring cakes, pies, cookies, whatever, coffee. A lot of the girls came down to see the soldiers so we'd give them an autograph and wish them good luck. Anyhow, from the beach patrol, that regiment was breaking up, and they had a lot of problems in some of the units that I'm not familiar with. But they broke it up, and we had a chance to choose where we went. We could go to the combat engineers, combat MPs, or we could go to an armored unit. And I chose the MPs. The MPs had some qualifications. You had to be six feet tall, you had to weigh so much, I can't remember now. But I chose that. And I went to a little post down in Delaware, Fort DuPont, Delaware. And it's right below Wilmington, named for the DuPont family, I suppose. But it was a coast artillery post. And we stayed there not very long. From there -- we were just training there, and from there we shipped overseas, went to Casablanca. But before --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Before we get too far in, talk about what a combat MP, what is the job of a combat MP and what does training entail?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Well, you have basically infantry training. Most of the people in combat MPs are qualified on small arms which includes up to the BAR, the Browning Automatic Rifle. And and what we did -- if I tell you what we did I think you'd understand better.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yes, please.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: We escorted troops, convoys. We established priorities of different vehicles, people, convoys at intersections. We ran straggler lines which was to stop people going both ways toward the front or from the front. And we did that. And we took over prisoners from infantry or whoever had them, they could turn them over to us and we'd take them back to the rear to the compounds. That was our biggest mission. But traffic control was a big mess. I don't know whether you ever saw the movie "Patton" or not, but there was a place in there, that movie, where I said to myself, goodness, I've done that a hundred times. It showed two or three or four convoys that came together at an intersection and they were stuck there. Nobody would make a decision of who should go first and who shouldn't. Well, a lot of officers tried to pull their rank and establish their priority. They wanted to get a convoy load of silk stockings to the front when there was a convoy of ambulances waiting behind them, that sort of thing. I exaggerated a little bit there but that's not too far-fetched. But we did that and just anything else that came that we were told to do.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Then further back from us, in the area further back from us was the station MPs where they -- like in Naples they set up a command and they had their own MPs. And then we worked with the corps MPs too. The corps MPs were smaller, though. There was only about one company of those to a corps and a corps is usually two or three divisions. And of course, we had many more than that. It was an interesting job. I spent most of my time on a motorcycle. And I escorted troops up and I escorted them back. Everything you could imagine. The trucks going north had rations on them, and ammunition, gasoline. But our officers kept us pretty well-informed as to who had priority. Also, you had to memorize a station list. You didn't carry any written locations of your units, so if you had the 212th tank destroyer was two miles down here and to the right through a pine thicket and so forth, you had to know these things. And as the vehicles got lost, and many of them did, didn't know their way around, you had to know where the units were located. And that was pretty tough. But you couldn't write it down. They won't let you do that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Let me ask you something. We might have jumped a little bit ahead. You go overseas from Fort DuPont, Delaware. Did you go down to New York to leave overseas?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yeah, left from Pier 82 on the MONTEREY.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And had you ever been on the ocean before?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Did you ever have any trouble with seasickness?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: No problem?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: How long did it take you to get across?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: I can't remember exactly. I know that the ship had continuous rotation for the mess hall. When you'd get a meal and get a chance to wash your mess kit out, it's time to get back in line again for the next meal. I don't remember how many men were on our ship, but I think it was probably 5,000. And I got -- I didn't want to ever get on the kitchen detail so I volunteered for the blackout detail. And I was a corporal at that time. And so I had a detail to take one section of the ship in the evening about dusk and put big curtains and blinds up so if somebody stepped out of the ship and lit a cigarette they wouldn't be seen. So we blacked out the whole ship that way every night.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Dual, two curtains?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Uh-huh, and then took them down in the morning.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Uh-huh. Now, were you guys in a convoy or --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yes -- no, we were by ourself. And one morning when we got up somebody was saying, you could hear them on deck coming up the ladder, look at that, the whole ship -- the whole ocean is covered with ships. And sure enough it was. When you looked out there was ships everywhere you could see. And right next to us was the battleship TEXAS and the bow of the TEXAS was going under the water. Beautiful thing to see.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I'll bet. As long as you don't get seasick.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: {Laughter} Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. So when you go over, do you -- where is the first place you land? Do you go straight to --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Casablanca.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You go straight to Casablanca.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: We got -- landed about 3- or 400 yards, we came in, it was behind the battleship JEAN BART that belonged to the Free French. And it had shot at the American Navy coming in. This was before us. We went in there at D plus -- D plus about four or five, I can't remember.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: We didn't make the initial landing.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: But the JEAN BART had a big hole in it that you could drive a truck through where the American Navy hit it, and it didn't get to fire but one salvo. They knocked it out.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: That's interesting. How did -- where did the French stay in at that time, D plus four?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: They were all ___. Part of them were Free French, part were Vichy French, part were under Petain and De Gaulle. But Mark Clark had made a trip over there earlier, and the French in Casablanca were our allies at that time. So it wasn't too bad.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So you get into Casablanca. What's your first impression of Casablanca?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Beautiful city.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Explain the terrain, what it's like.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Well, the terrain was neither flat or hilly. I'd say just a rolling, pleasant terrain. And from the port up to the main part of town was sort of like the slums. It was the Arab section. They called those medinas. And when you got up to town, which is not very far, it's just like being in France. The buildings and streets, everything looks like France. It's a beautiful place. We stayed in an opera house that was right in the center of town. And it was a real convenient place for us to stay because it had a lot of room. And there was a bandstand in a courtyard there at this theater, and so -- or opera house or theater. And that was a great place to put the kitchen because it could rain or whatever and the kitchen could go right on, didn't have to put up the kitchen flys and that sort of thing.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: But we had a chance to sleep inside. We had spent the first two nights on the beach. And the beach was not sandy where we stayed, it was rocky. It was on in about 4- or 500 yards and it was miserable. The guys made all kinds of comments, I always wanted to live on the beach, and that sort of thing. But finally we got up to the opera house. So they told us, you guys can find yourself a bunk in there. So we let these -- we went in and it was a beautiful place, had all the gold ornaments and decorations and large chandeliers and this sort of thing. And all the seating in it were red velvet, just beautiful. So we took the seats out, laid them down on the floor and made bunks out of them. And so we had it made. We stayed inside nice and warm with a good night's sleep and all that. And everybody got up the next morning, they were yelling and scratching and screaming and cursing and this sort of thing. And you wonder what in the world happened. Well, what happened was that all that red velvet cushions were full of fleas.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Oh, man.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: {Laughter} So we had B Company of 101st Military Police Battalion flea-bitten. And that's probably the first casualties of war that I've ever heard of from a flea. But that happened.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: {Laughter} Okay, so we're in Casablanca. We just talked about the police. How long did you stay in the opera house? How long were you actually there?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: In that particular place, probably about two to three weeks, something like that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And then what were you doing during the day?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: During the day we were looking for the German prisoners, the German officers who were living so well out along the coast. Out along the coast going south towards Marrakech, there was beautiful homes on the beach very similar to what we have in this country. It was a resort area. And a lot of German officers moved out there and were in those quarters. So we'd go out there and pick them up and bring them back and put them in the PW compound. We had a large PW compound there in Casablanca because everybody that we found, some of the troops, some of our people were going in vehicles out in the desert, and they'd go by tips, the Arabs would tip off where the Germans were and that sort of thing, and they'd go out and get them there. Now, we were not fighting in there. The Germans knew the war was over for them so we didn't get in any fire fights with them or anything like that. We'd go out along the beach there, and many times we came to a beach house and they'd be drunk, ready to surrender. And they'd have their uniforms neatly packed and they'd be in civilian clothes. There's all sorts of -- they'd be in their shorts or bathing trunks. You know, it was no big deal. But after the -- besides that we --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Talk about the grasshoppers.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Oh, okay. The grasshoppers, I never heard of a grasshopper storm except the stories that the Mormon told about the locusts coming in and eating the crops. But one day we were out in the boondocks there from Casablanca probably five to ten miles. And we were in an open weapons carrier, a Dodge weapons carrier, half-ton, and we had the windshield folded down. Beautiful weather over there, cruising along with the windshield down. Just nice weather, good place to be, good day to be alive. And all at once something went splat and started hitting us in the face. And it was this green gooey stuff that came out of great big grasshoppers, huge things. And more and more started hitting us, we couldn't keep them off enough. You couldn't keep your hands up like this to avoid all of them. So we stopped and we had to almost get under the vehicle, the fenders, to keep the grasshoppers from flying in to us. But those things were coming, you could look out, and there was like a dust storm, thousands of them. And so we finally made it in a little closer to the village, to the medinas where the Arabs were. And they were running around with their -- they'd take their garment that they wear, I don't know the name of it, they'd pull it up like this and make a sack out of it like an apron. And they were filling that thing full of grasshoppers as fast as they could pick them up, and they were scooping them up from the curb and the gutter with their hands and putting them in there as fast as they could. And they were grabbing boxes and tin cans and everything they could put grasshoppers in. So they harvested those grasshoppers. And then for the next few days you'd see these people selling grasshoppers on the street. They'd have a tray, like wooden tray with a strap on it, and they'd be mounded up with grasshoppers, and they'd sell you so many grasshoppers for so much money. And the people that bought the grasshoppers were eating them just like popcorn. And we even saw the kids who had eaten those live ones that had just died or expired, they were eating them the same way. The ones that went splat on us, those kids were eating them. So it was a very popular thing. The Arabs love those grasshopper storms, I suppose.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Did you try it?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: No, we didn't try it.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: It's like raining gumdrops or whatever. {Laughter}

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: No, we didn't try that. And then from Casablanca we went -- started a convoy north and we went on up through to Algiers, up in that area. We went to a place called Ojdua, O-j-d-u-a, something like that. And we were fortunate enough, my platoon, to get to stay around where Mark Clark put his headquarters, the Fifth Army headquarters. So we got to stay around there for a while. And it was pretty good duty. It was just plain guard duty, nothing else, and it was real easy.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Guarding basically Mark Clark --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: The headquarters.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: The headquarters?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yes, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And explain what this -- what a typical day is like, then, in this duty. A typical army day, you get up early, you go on call for a while, and then you just have the rest of the time to yourself or what?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Well, it was really sort of like training. We pitched pyramidal tents and made a tent city, a company city. And of course with regulations, you put so many tents in this row and then in this row so many feet apart. And so we had pyramidal tent city. And then the officers are off about a hundred feet from us, the mess hall between the officers and enlisted men. And the mess hall was in a -- we call it a kitchen screen, but it's like a big tent and you roll the sides up to give the cooks a little ventilation. And then we haul gravel a lot in the daytime. We found a place we can get gravel, and we'd take our vehicles out there and haul gravel and put it in our company street and beautify the place and just make it a lot nicer. But what it did, looking at it from the officer's and NCO's standpoint, it kept the troops busy. You know, you can't let troops stay idle, you just don't do that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: And we got to go swimming quite a bit in the Mediterranean, and then pulled guard duty mostly at night. They had one or two guards during the daytime but at nighttime they triple or double it, just to keep the Arabs out mostly. Arabs were beggars. And you couldn't blame them with the oil, and the Nazis took everything they could take when they left there. And so that's about it. You pulled the guard duty when it was your turn about every fourth or fifth day. We weren't needed that bad. And then I think the Fifth Army was in the planning stages at that time. We moved from there and went further north to a town called Arzew, and it's -- Arzew is just east of Bizerte. Bizerte -- anyhow, we went to Arzew and we started waterproofing our vehicles. So that's what we did. We worked with that Cosmoline which is a waterproofing grease. Put that on all the vehicles so it didn't break down with saltwater when you unloaded it, if you unloaded it in water. So we waterproofed our vehicles there and tried to stay out of the hot sun as much as we could. With that hot grease on your hands and your shoulders, you couldn't keep from getting it on your body. We'd work until the sun would get up toward noon and we'd load the trucks up and go to the ocean. And we'd go to the ocean and we could clean up, frolic around, swim. And we didn't do anything until the next day because it's too hot.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Had you done any landing training up to this point?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Oh, yes, yes. That was fitting in there too.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. I mean, you would feel comfortable as far as --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yeah. Well, our training was different from most other training. We had -- I mentioned this priority type thing to you. We had -- to work the beaches, we worked lands. The engineers would sap the beach probing for land mines or any kind of mine, personnel mine or whatever, and they'd put the engineer tape along the sides. And the thing we had to do was keep the vehicles coming in, bring them in between the lines and put them on the road they're supposed to go on to meet their unit. And then occasionally we'd run across somebody that was either dumb or a smarty, and he would turn his vehicle and start down the beach, and when he did that he could hit a mine anywhere, not staying between the lines. And we had to watch for that and see that it didn't happen. I said I wasn't going to tell any blood and guts stories but I'm going to tell one here that is highly unusual. We were -- the beach was being bombed one day. The Stukas were coming in between two hills, mounds like that, and they come in between them and come down the beach before we -- real quick, you'd hardly know they were on top of you. And we had a lieutenant named Harrell, and he was out on the beach and we were up in the dunes. Before, I was up there taking a break. And we could see him down there, but an air raid started and we could see the planes coming, but we couldn't make him hear us, there was just too much noise. And they were bombing that beach, and when they dropped the bomb it hit right where he had been. And we never did find a piece of him, not even a dog tag, not a boot, nothing. We didn't find anything at all. And he was listed as missing in action, which he was, but of course he was dead. But we got off -- I got off my subject there a little bit. We were talking about the invasion training and so forth?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Well, we went from Arzew, we massed there in the harbor of Bizerte, and we had some air raids there. And there were so many ships in the harbor it looked a turn of fire going up in the air shooting at the German bombers. Just an awful lot of fire power, and that was only for a couple of nights. And then we left from there and went to Salerno.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Now, at this point are you seeing quite a bit of German bombers or German fighters or had the Americans got air superiority in the area?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: No, not quite a bit. The German bombers you'd only see at night. And I don't recall more than a couple of air raids at night. Now, in the daytime I mentioned awhile ago coming from Casablanca up to -- I don't remember if we stopped at ___. Anyhow, going up through the desert there, you'd get strafed occasionally. And that was ME-109s, I guess, and we kept a pretty good watch for them. We didn't have a whole lot of casualties from the strafing. And they were mostly looking for -- well, they were looking for anything they could hit, but what they really liked to find was the armor.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Was the armor -- where was it --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: It was in convoy.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So is that -- I mean, did you guys have armor with you?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: No, we had no armor.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Where was the Third Army at this time, do you know?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: It wasn't the Third Army at that time, it was called I Armored Corps. It wasn't known by the press by that name, but it was Patton's army. In the army anything with an "I" designation is provisional, and so I Armored Corps was formed there and Patton took that armor and his armored divisions into that. And I think the Third Division was in that too, the infantry division. And they went up and got in some pretty good fights. Where the first bayonet fighting of the war occurred was up in that area in a place called Hill 609, and there was some bayonet fighting up there with the Third Division. But we were never involved in anything like that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You guys were down in Bizerte harbor, did you say?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And then are you preparing at this time, have they set you up or do you know where you're going to be going?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. But do you know that you are going to be --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: We just knew we were going somewhere to make an invasion but we didn't know where. We thought Sicily, but Sicily had already been invaded.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Well, how do you feel at this time, then? Are you starting to get nervous, are you scared? What's your feeling when you know you're about to make your first really combat landing? Or do you know it's going to be a combat landing?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: I don't want to sound heroic or brave or anything, I don't mean it that way, but I was having a ball, I was having the time of my life.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: I was a little country boy from Knoxville, never been anywhere, never seen anything. And so anything I saw and did was new and different to me.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right, okay. Well, let's work on to the landing, then. How long are you actually this the harbor before you --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Overnight. We came in there during the darkness and anchored offshore. And the next morning, which was about D plus two, I guess, we were standing on the deck of this ship, this liberty ship. Before I say that I want to say something about going over there. You could look down and see the bottom of the ocean all the way from Bizerte over there. The Mediterranean was as blue and pretty as you had ever seen. It didn't look like the ocean.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: It looked like somebody's fine swimming pool. But anyhow, we were standing on the deck there and there were several of us just waiting for the bags to be brought through the hold to unload and take in, and somebody said, there comes some airplanes. And another fellow said, yep, those P38s are beautiful, aren't they? And there was an old English officer standing right beside us within earshot, and he said, son, you better look again, those are not P38s. And by that time those planes had gotten closer, and they came in a dive. And I've often heard that they had the sirens on their wings. I think these probably did but I can't remember that clearly. And they came in and unloaded, and their bombs were hitting within -- I guess the closest one to us was a hundred feet. But docked -- not docked, moored, I guess you would say in the navy, stopped next to us was the battleship SAVANNAH. Not a battleship, it was the cruiser SAVANNAH, and it was not too far offshore. And it was firing, firing their five-inch guns, supporting the infantry or tanks or whatever, but in support. And one of those bombs hit that ship, and when it did, you could see those gun turners going up through the air tumbling like that. But a strange thing -- of course we hit the deck then, we were out of sight because it was too hot to stand on deck looking. But anyhow, as the noise died down the planes were further away and so forth. Somebody said, well, will you look at that. And we got up and looked, and there was a crate of oranges intact, not broken open, squeezed, mashed or anything. A crate of oranges blew off the SAVANNAH onto our ship.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: {Laughter}

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Now that's a war story. That's the kind you tell at the bar to win another round. But it's true. We later -- pardon me, I got to -- {drinking water} Somebody got a magazine from home two or three months later and it had the story of the ship getting hit there, and it said 51 sailors were killed. Of course, it wasn't have been so funny about the oranges if we had known they lost their life.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right, yeah. Did you say -- there were a lot of ships in that --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Was anyone else hit in there? I mean, did you take ___+.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: What he did -- we were watching him. He started it looked like full power for the shore forward, he was facing the shore. And then he stopped and then he reversed and went back out into deeper water. We thought -- somebody there, I don't know anything about the navy, but they thought he was going to beach the ship because it hit that hard. Not much damage so we thought he was going to beach it. But he didn't, he maneuvered back out. But there was a lot of navy support at Salerno. And the reason was, eight miles in there was a town named Battipaglia, and it was held pretty firm by the Germans for three or four days. And they -- we didn't have our armor ashore, we didn't have our tanks ashore, and we weren't making much of an impact on Battipaglia. And it was right on the road to Naples, we had to go through it. So they almost lost it, but they got the armor ashore and after a couple days they took it. But a lot of casualties, awfully heavy. And two miles west of Battipaglia back towards the beach there was a river there, and I can't remember whether it was Sele or Volturno. But anyhow, we were up above where the engineers were putting a Bailey bridge in to get the armor across. They had blown out the old bridge. There was a railroad bridge up above there and my platoon was guarding that railroad bridge. This came to mind awhile ago when you asked me if we did any combat and so forth. We just did jobs like that when called to do it.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: And we had a 50-caliber machine gun up there, that's all we had. If there had been some of those German tanks coming down that railroad track we would have probably let them have that machine gun.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: {Laughter}

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: I say that in jest, of course.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I know, I'm sure. Now, once you come on in Salerno, and you say that's what, D plus two, D plus three? Howard Finley Bolton Something like that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: How far had the lines advanced to this point by the time you get on there? Are they all the way to Battipaglia?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: They had passed that. We went through Battipaglia, and it was completely demolished, it was just completely demolished. And I remember that town well because one of our sergeants delivered a baby there. But anyhow, they were far above that, and there were several towns to go through between there and Naples. But that was the goal, to get Naples, because we needed the harbor and the Germans bombed the harbor pretty heavily. When we got there the harbor was pretty well demolished. We had to go through several little towns there. The first one was Nola, and then we came to Marigliano, Pomigliano, and then another one before Naples, I can't recall the name. But anyhow, those towns were not torn up much and they went through there pretty easily. They tore up the main buildings, like the municipal buildings were torn up. And I don't know whether they were being held by the Germans or whether some tankers were just trying to get in some gun practice. But that's the way they went to Naples. And the Germans did not try to hold Naples too long because they had already done what they wanted to do, and that was to tear the harbor up.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. Now, as you're coming through here, you said obviously that a baby was born in one of the towns there.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What about civilians or refugees coming through there?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Those refugees would hide most anywhere they could hide. But many refugees were pretty smart as to what to do. They had lived with war for many years. They went to the little towns that were off the beaten path. The American army stayed on the main thoroughfares; Highway 60, Highway 65, these were main roads. They would be -- you might compare it to Highway 41 from Chattanooga to Knoxville. They stayed on that road. Well, the refugees would get off the side roads and these little small towns up in the hills, and there were a lot of those in Italy. And they would hide until the Germans were gone. Then when we came in, we usually had some guy with us that's called the AMGOT-er. The AMGOT stood for American Allied Military Government, but the abbreviation is spelled AMGOT. But anyhow, they'd go and find the mayor and the councilmen and so forth and tell the people what was going on and they were safe. But a lot of the refugees would come out and get on the roads. And one of our main jobs all during the war was keeping those refugees off the road so we could get our equipment through. And our drivers, it don't matter how brave, tough, tough they are, are not going to run over women and children with a truck.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: And we had to keep it clear. And I used to have a piece of rubber that I'd hold out from my motorcycle handlebar here, and I'd ride along the side right on the shoulder and sort of tap them along there to get their attention and keep them off the road. But then you had to put up with the oxcarts and the old cars and the charcoal-fired trucks that they had, and it was really a big mess. And then we'd establish points, straggler points, where we would search everybody going north or south, either way, and we'd see who they were. We got a lot of German prisoners out of those people and a lot of Italian soldiers deserted. And they were supposed to be on our side at that time. Most of them wanted to go home, they were not really deserters. But a lot of Germans got in that mix. And what we'd have to do was pull their clothing back to see what they were wearing and look for tattoos. And speaking the language was the easiest way to tell. We had enough people in the company that came from those National Guard units up there in Jersey with Italian descent that spoke Italian pretty well, and they could weed out the Germans and whoever out of those crowds of people pretty easy. But that was one of our hardest jobs. It was a thankless job. You'd be standing there 12 to 14 hours doing the same thing all the time.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: These people are hungry, right? I mean --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Sure, they were hungry. Little kids in those buggies and stuff. A lot of it was heartbreaking.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Uh-huh. Were the Americans able to help at all with food or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Most Americans gave away their darn food. They gave away their C rations, K rations or whatever they could spare. They would reach in their gas mask, that's where you hid the contraband, the candy and cigarettes and everything, you put it in your gas mask. The gas mask is the easy way to carry it.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Secret's out.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: {Laughter} So, yeah, particularly they'd give the kids something, they'd give the kids something to eat. But we didn't always have something to eat ourself. But I made -- I never did get hungry over there. I don't think I could get hungry in this country.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So are you stationed, then -- where are you stationed? Do you move all the way up into Naples?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: We bypass Naples.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You bypass Naples.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: And one platoon went to a town called Caserta and stayed in the king's castle in Caserta. My platoon went to the next town up the road seven miles named Santa Maria, and we stayed in the city hall, second floor, marble floor. Tough to sleep on. And then the other platoon went north of there to a little town called Venafro. Venafro is four or five miles from Cassino. You've heard of Cassino and Montecatini and all that. Then we went through a winter there, the winter of '43, I guess it was. And then they pulled out of our -- each platoon, they pulled about 12 men to go to Anzio, and so they went to Anzio. And the same thing up there. But back to the Cassino front. We were stationed there a long time, but we did an awful lot of escort work with convoys, trucks and so forth because we were still close to the -- to Naples. And all the supplies were being unloaded there; hospitals, gasoline, anything you could think of to support a moving army. And so we were stockpiling it up toward the front. So we were pretty busy with that. That particular time I stayed in a little town, Santa Maria there, and I had a real busy intersection, a little cobblestone right about the middle of town. And three of us worked that for, I think it was two months. We were at it daily for two months. If one of us wanted a day off the other guys cover for them.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Explain how rank works here, rank versus you being with -- an MP. How does that work if it comes down to a confrontation?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Well, it just depends on what the confrontation is. You better be right. If you're an MP you better be right. And your officers back you up. If you're told to hold all deuce -- six-by-six convoys, if you're told to hold them to let tank retrievers through or things, well, that's what you do. So if anybody says anything, your own CO is the one that's doing it, he has to back you up. But as far as rank was never a problem that -- I ran into a lieutenant once that gave me a little flack but it was nothing major. I never had any problem with it. Most everything we were doing was helping people.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: We were not the enemy.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: So we really didn't have any problem.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. Okay. So during this time, then, you said you worked like two months straight without really even taking a day off.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So were you just working and sleeping, is that basically it?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Once again, are you eating C rations? Are you getting anything from town or --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Anything I can get. Once they put us on a -- three of us on motorcycles, because we were the only ones that could get there. It was a real muddy intersection. We were about ten miles from the company and the company was in bivouac, and it was raining. We pitched as much shelter as we could. And we got all of our rations off the trucks that were coming through. A lot of times we'd just stop a truck and go around and see what he was hauling. If he had five-and-one rations or ten-and-one rations we'd take a case of them. They didn't -- nobody seemed to mind. We never got court-martialed for taking groceries to eat ourself. If you took two cases you might be in trouble. {Laughter}

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. So, now, you say you're working this intersection. You say you're doing a lot of escort work.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Explain what your escort -- who you're escorting or what you're doing.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Well, we weren't escorting from that intersection. Information and directing traffic is what we were doing, because so many people couldn't get through that intersection. It was narrow and it was mud that deep.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: And everything was sort of at a stalemate on the front. And there was not a lot of personnel convoys or not a lot of -- not a lot of people coming back and not a lot going forward, just sort of a stalemate.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right, stagnant.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: But it was miserable duty because of the weather, because it was so muddy. And you can't change clothes. You know, most of us went two, three, four months without taking a bath or changing clothes. We were pretty lousy soldiers. You were scratching either your top or your bottom all the time. You had to scratch somewhere.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: {Laughter}. {End of tape}

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: {Interruption} -- about the refugees coming down. Were there many Germans surrendering at this point in the war?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: No, there was not many Germans surrendering. Most of the German surrenders came by units. Very few individuals did. But most of the German prisoners that we saw were in large groups.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Like in North Africa?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yes. In North Africa we handled thousands and thousands of Germans prisoners that were being brought down from up in Bizerte, up in that area, where Rommel's army had surrendered. And they loaded them on the trains, the old French 40 and eight cattle cars, 40 men or eight horses, famous from World War I. And they brought those cars down to Casablanca where they put them on boats. But they had a long trip across the desert in those trains, and this was in the heat of the year, it was in the summertime. We did what we call a prisoner stop. And what we would do, the train would come down to a point and stop, and we'd put up lister bags. And these lister bags were full of water where you could fill a canteen. And we filled the lister bags from trailers that we had, 550-gallon trailers. And we'd have them get off the trains and we let the German officers, tell the German officers what to do, our officers would tell the German officers. The German officers would tell their non-coms what to do. And they'd have formations. Prisoners would get off of the train and they'd put them in formation like a platoon and then they'd march them down to our slit trenches. And we had slit trenches prepared, dug about that deep, a foot to 18 inches deep, in a straight line for, oh, hundreds of feet. And as the prisoners would come down the non-coms would march down and they'd use the slit trench to relieve themselves. And when they would finish they would cover that slit trench. Then we'd have them dig another one six to eight feet from that one, and then the one that they just covered would be marked along that it was opened a certain date and closed a certain date. So that's how we used for sanitation. We also fed them while we were there. We'd give them two cans of C rations, one would either be hash, beans or stew are the only three choices then, and a can of biscuits to go with it. And they'd let them exercise some. We let the non-coms do this. And all we'd do is stand around with the machine guns, submachine guns, and we'd go through the trains to see what was in there. Mostly we'd find dead Germans. They'd get suffocated in there or they'd get trampled to death. They got down on the floor way to try to get a little more air by sticking their nose in between those slats. And somebody would be standing on top of them for hours. You know, they'd pass out from exposure or whatever. But we always took several dead Germans off those trains when they stopped there. And then we just reversed the procedure; when they were finished, put them back on the train. We had guards -- somebody else put the guards up there, not our people, on top of the trains. And they'd go on to Casablanca and another train would come and we'd do the same thing.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Then in Anzio, they had them digging down in Anzio for burying the dead. They'd bury the German dead down there. And the GR people were in charge of that, graves restoration, which is part of the Quartermaster Corps. They'd take charge of that. And of course all we did was guard the prisoners. But they did that other places. Now, I also got prisoners when the war was over up north of Modina in Italy. They'd surrender as a unit, a whole regiment of Germans would surrender. And we'd use their trucks, their convoys, and take them to Modina to a compound, a prisoner of war compound. And many times I'd find a good way to do it. I'd put my motorcycle on the vehicle and I'd ride in the staff car up front. And that worked out pretty well. I got to know a lot of those German commanders. They spoke English pretty well. We could communicate what time were we going to eat and all that stuff. But that wasn't bad duty. The war was over, everybody was going home. Even those German prisoners were nice. They knew the war was over.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. The ones you saw in North Africa, though, were they particularly cocky or --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Hostile and cocky and arrogant, yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I've heard that about Rommel's --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yeah, they were. Well, they weren't convinced they'd lost the war. But those up in Italy, they knew the war was lost.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. The last we talked you were in Santa Maria, and then eventually you move up --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: I move on up through Italy. And the winter of '44 was terrible as far as the weather was concerned. And we stayed in a town north of Florence about 35 to 40 miles in the mountains, and we stayed in a little place off Route 6529, I can't remember the name of the little town. But anyway, we stayed in a little Catholic church there, a school and church combined. There was about four nuns there and they had about 15 orphans in there. And we occupied the bottom, the basement, just one platoon of us. At that time we had -- we had to guard the top of the pass at night so vehicles didn't try to come down this mountain, because if they did they'd get killed, they'd slide off that ice over the side of the mountain. But we had to stay up there at night, and that's the duty we performed. And we had four parkas up there to go around, so when you went on duty you were warm, when you came off duty you froze until you went back on. The equipment, the good equipment we had in World War II didn't get to us until the war was over. {Laughter} I don't mean that as sour grapes. Anyhow, that's the way it was. Can I run just a brief story about that?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: We played checkers down in the basement. And we had a boy from south Georgia that was the checker champion of the whole company, he could beat anybody. And we had some British people down below us, and we got along fine with them. They'd come up to see us and we borrowed their skis and this sort of thing. And we got a contest going around there with checkers. And a little kid that lived in that orphanage watched this checker game for several days or weeks, and one day he wanted to play. And the guys, just to humor the kid said, okay, play. I'll make this long story short. Between the British and the Americans and an engineer company that was down below us on down the hill, there was probably 6-, 700 troops up there on the side of that mountain. That kid beat everybody that they could bring up there.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: {Laughter}

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Everybody. And he couldn't have been more than eleven. He could have been ten years old, somewhere between nine and eleven. But he beat everybody in checkers. And I'll never forget that. Fantastic.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: That's funny. We need to find out that was because ___+ somebody.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Now, you stayed there for the winter of '44.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Stayed there the winter of '44, then we went on up and brought the prisoners back, as I mentioned before. And then waited and waited and waited under the point system to come home. And we got home --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Hold on, now. You were in Rome too, right?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Oh, yes, I was in Rome.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Talk about your time in Rome.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Well, Rome is where I had this disaster I mentioned to you before I didn't like. We stayed in a place in Rome called Fiero Mussolini. And Fiero means fair, and they were going to have a world's fair in this compound. And they had built all these Olympic-sized pools, tracks for track and field meets, but they'd also put numbers of beautiful statues all around these different places. And the statutes came from the alabaster and marble that's produced just south of Rome, a little -- I can't remember the name of the town offhand, but it isn't important. Anyhow, this is a very pretty place. Some of the people in the company got to go down to the Tiber. We were north of the Vatican. They got to go down to the Tiber, down to the river to the Vatican and meet the Pope. And the whole company went at the same time, they blessed their flag and all that. I'm not Catholic so I didn't go. But anyhow, that was something for those guys to remember. I'm sure it was a highlight of the war for them. I didn't get downtown too much because I worked right at the Coliseum for at least two days, maybe more. I directed traffic right there at the corner of that Coliseum. And I thought so many times, you people spend a fortune all over the world to come see this hunk of stone up here and here I am sitting on my butt eating K rations. {Laughter} So I didn't appreciate the Coliseum that much, but I did direct traffic there an awful long time.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: After you left, though, did you appreciate, I mean, just the age of it?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: No, no. I didn't particularly like Italy.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: They just did a lot of things I didn't approve of.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Like the women that would fraternize with the Germans, they'd cut their hair off and all, but they didn't do anything to the men. What did they do to the men that fraternized with the Germans? Nothing. A lot of things like that that I didn't care for.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Uh-huh. Now, at this point, then, you say the points are starting to kick in and people are starting to go home.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So are you just waiting four your points to come in?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Went to Florence.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So you go to Florence.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Went to Florence and stayed about a month. And I had a half-ton recon station, recon car that a guy gave me that was going home. So I had another fellow there with me from up here in Cleveland, Tennessee named Jesse Pullan, and we toured Italy because we were waiting for the points to come in that they put on the bulletin board, so you'd just have to check the bulletin board once a day. We went over to the leaning tower and all over that part of Italy, we just toured around. But we had to be back every day so we took short trips and just bided our time waiting for our name to come on the bulletin board. Finally it did. And then we went on a liberty ship. And it was 19 days, I believe, I don't know how I could forget it, but it was 19 days at least. And on that liberty ship we had three movies on there, and we saw those three movies every night over and over.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: {Laughter} Do you remember the movies?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yes, I do.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What were they?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Humphrey Bogart in "High Sierra", the "Tale of Two Cities", and Humphrey Bogart in "The Fugitive", I think it was. It don't come to mind right now. I'm sure of those two.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Have you seen them since?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Oh, no.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: {Laughter}

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: {Laughter} No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. So you finally get home.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Got home.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And then are you planning to make this a career now?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: No. I was discharged at Camp Atterbury, Indiana, came back to Knoxville. Everything had changed so much. I had been gone almost five years. And I started working on the railroad where my dad had worked. And I was a brakeman on the L and N Railroad for about nine months, something like that. And I wasn't too steady at working -- I was on an extra board. On the railroad extra board is when you don't have enough seniority to hold a regular scheduled run, they call you as they need you. What they did was hire too many men returning from the war and the extra board was loaded so you didn't get but about two runs a month. And I couldn't live on that. And my wife was pregnant and I said --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Your wife. When did you meet your wife? How soon after you got back?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Very soon.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Did you know her before?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: No, no, I didn't.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Let me -- let me continue with this railroad thing here for a second. So they'd have it -- things did look better and we were running pretty regular on the road. They'd have a coal strike and they'd do the same thing to us. And during these strikes I was trying to make money any way I could. And over where we lived in North Knoxville, it was a smoky part of town from the railroads. A lot of houses over there, and you couldn't buy paint during the war. People would have their houses washed. And so I was washing those big old two-story houses over there standing on top of a ladder with soap running down my arm, cold. And I decided this is not the way to make a living. And I decided I'd go back in the army. And Frances and I talked about it, and she said whatever you want to do, and so that's what I did, I went back in. And from then I've been stationed in, oh, probably eight to ten different states and I've traveled through I'd say 15 to 20 foreign countries all over the world. And then we came back from Heidelberg, Germany in 1962 to Fort Campbell, Kentucky. And I had five children, and they told me that I was going to have to take jump training. Well, I decided with 22 years of service and five children I didn't need to be jumping out of airplanes and so I retired.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. Now, let's move back to your family. You meet your wife shortly after the war. Do you remember what you were doing when you meet her? What's her name?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Frances.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Frances, okay. You say you met her walking in Oak Ridge. Walking or working?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Working.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Working, all right. And then when you join the service, when do you get into the nuclear program?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: It's odd how that happened. I'd always been interested in photography. When I wanted to reenlist and come out to Oak Ridge, Tennessee, I went out there to see a fellow that I had known as a kid, and he said, I've got one vacancy out here that I can put you in and it's in the ID section. And he said all you do is run a little camera. So I went out there and talked to the colonel, and he said, I'd be glad to have you. Anyhow, I reenlisted for Oak Ridge, I was stationed there. My daughter, Jeri, was born over there in Oak Ridge. And I stayed there until they decided to ship all the military out, it was about a year. And I had chance to go to photographer school at Fort Norman so I went to photographer school. From photographer school, because of my clearance and my background and I still knew this colonel from Oak Ridge, I got into the nuclear weapons program at Sandy base -- no, in Los Alamos, photographing integral parts of handling equipment and components of nuclear weapons to be used for training manuals and for use for teaching, like made slides and that sort of thing. And I enjoyed that. I stayed with that three or four years. And I was promoted as high as I could go. I was promoted to staff sergeant -- or tech sergeant. Staff or tech, I can't remember which. But anyhow, I couldn't go any higher in rank. That's what the table of organization said I could do.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: So I said, well, if I can't do that, I've been around these weapons all this time I might as well go for that, so I started going to weapons schools. I went to 21 different orientation courses and schools on nuclear weapons over my career, and I worked on the nuclear weapons. And at one time I was a crew chief, a mechanical crew chief assembling the weapons and handling the weapons and moving them in and out of storage and in and out of aircraft and that sort of thing. And then I got into the electronic side of it and became a nuclear weapons electronics officer. And I did that at White Sands, New Mexico. And in between here I was operations sergeant up at Pueblo Ordinance Depot. We were handling the nuclear components for the artillery pieces.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: And I just decided to go nuclear, and that left me a lot of longevity in that program. I had been in the program a long time. And I had a colonel that I worked -- he wasn't a colonel, he was a major that I worked for all this time practically, his name was Sullivan from Tuckahoe, New Jersey(sic), and he encouraged me to become a warrant officer. I told him I didn't particularly want it because I was going to retire so that I had my time in. And I was a master sergeant then. And then anyhow, he encouraged me to do that, so I applied for it and got it. And as a warrant officer I continued to do about the same thing I did as a master sergeant. Very little difference. And so I went to a unit down in White Sands, New Mexico, and had a crew there. And they were getting ready to go overseas, so I went to Germany with them. And I had a crew down in a storage facility where we stored nuclear weapons, and brought my family over there. And they needed a -- they needed a warrant officer up in Eighth Army headquarters on the inspection team, the IG inspection team to inspect nuclear units. And there was an awful lot of warrant officers that had more rank than me but nobody had any more experience than I did, and so I was selected for that. And I stayed in the inspections division up there until I decided to come back home.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Talk about your safety record.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Well, I had a wonderful safety record, the whole program. I'm very proud of the -- something we could never talk about or publicize, but we probably had the greatest safety record of anybody that ever handled munitions of any kind. All these nuclear weapons that we had, many of them that we took to sea with us on the aircraft carriers -- and incidentally, we got involved in that too, and we moved them around the country like on maneuvers. We'd take live weapons, these were war reserve weapons, we'd take those out in the fields, out in the woods in Louisiana or wherever, and we handled those weapons, took them apart, put them together, performed maintenance. And they could be very dangerous if you didn't handle them properly.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: But we taught safety so well and we were all safety conscious, that we never had a nuclear accident of any sort. In fact, we never had a high explosive accident of any sort. And I was always very proud of that record because I don't think anybody else could -- any other unit ever did that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Uh-huh, all right. Now, what you were in -- during the Korean war what were you doing? Where were you --

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Well, what happened there is all of us in the nuclear weapons program had what was known as a Q clearance, it's a very high clearance, it's a little above top secret. We were frozen to the United States because they didn't want you to get captured, possibly captured, so we didn't have to go overseas. And it was a pretty good deal for us, really. But the thinking was it compensated us for the increased training that we had to do.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: But they lifted that. No longer had to stay in the States. When they did, the army was hurting so much for people in Korea, they had some great losses in Korea at that time, that they took everybody that had a nuclear weapons MOS and hadn't been overseas recently, and we all went. And when we went, I went in a terrible unit. I went into a unit that didn't have any discipline, it didn't have morale, it was a terrible unit. And they had a new CO came in, and they had a non-com unit, a non-commissioned officers meeting, and he said he was going to change that unit and shape it up. And he said, who wants to be first sergeant. Well, at that time I was a tech sergeant, and nobody raised their hand out of all those non-coms. And I don't blame -- some of them were non-coms that had a lot of combat duty and eligible for retirement and they didn't want that weighted load. And everybody could see it was a big job, it was going to be tough to do, so I raised my hand. And he said, I want you to come talk to me, and I did. And I was promoted in a couple days to first sergeant until I left, 18 months. And I had a good unit, I had a wonderful unit. And I was -- it was probably the best job I had all the time I was in the army.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
sp.p: Yeah. I mentioned to you back some time ago that the Camp Croft, South Carolina had this first sergeant that I talked so much about, Sergeant Withers was his name. And I always wanted to be like Sergeant Withers. I tried to run my company in Korea like Sergeant Withers. And when I got on the boat I don't think I owed anybody an apology.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. You say it was the best job you had. The most satisfying?

sp.speaker: Howard Finley Bolton
